written.myAnswer: Flammable liquids should not be stored in ordinary refrigerators because a spark from the refrigerator’s thermostat may ignite their vapours and cause a fire or explosion.
Explosive chemicals may explode if exposed to sudden shock, heat or friction.
Neutralize the acid and alkali waste, then flush it down the drain with plenty of water, following the laboratory’s disposal instructions.
Examples include hydrofluoric acid (HF), caustic alkalis such as sodium hydroxide, and glacial acetic acid.

Use only a small quantity under the teacher’s supervision; keep it away from heat, shock and friction; wear suitable protective equipment; and keep other people and unnecessary materials away. Follow the laboratory’s instructions for handling and disposal.
Reactive chemicals can cause fires or explosions, release hazardous gases, and injure people or damage property if handled improperly.
Keep radioactive sources shielded and minimize the time spent near them; keep as much distance from the source as practicable.
Asphyxiant chemicals include carbon monoxide and hydrogen cyanide, as well as oxygen-displacing gases such as nitrogen, argon, helium, methane and carbon dioxide.
Carry out reactions or experiments that produce hazardous vapours, especially toxic or corrosive vapours, in a fume cupboard.

Explosive chemicals can release heat, gas and pressure suddenly, causing severe injury, fire or property damage. Toxic chemicals can poison the body through exposure and may cause serious illness or death.

Examples of toxic chemicals include mercury, benzene, chlorine, pesticides and hydrogen cyanide. A toxic gas spreading in the laboratory can poison people, cause breathing difficulties or unconsciousness, and may lead to death.

Warn others and alert the teacher; keep people away and do not touch or move the spill or its container. Follow the laboratory emergency procedure and let trained personnel deal with the spill. If anyone is exposed, flush the affected area with running water and seek medical attention.

Transport chlorine only in suitable, secure containers and use properly maintained equipment. Inspect containers and fittings regularly, train workers in safe handling, and prepare an emergency response plan. If a leak occurs, warn people, move them away from the affected area, and call trained emergency responders.
